## Who this is for

`melbfoot` is for people who plan around foot traffic in central Melbourne,
such as a café owner deciding when to open or an event planner choosing a time
and place. It helps you answer one question:

> When are the most people walking past my location, and how much has foot
> traffic changed since 2025?

The package includes hourly pedestrian counts from the City of Melbourne
Pedestrian Counting System, two functions that summarise them, and a Shiny app.

## Install

Install the package from GitHub:

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("ETC5523-2026/etc5523-assignment-4-inayat-gill")
```

## Launch the app

```{r launch, eval = FALSE}
library(melbfoot)
launch_app()
```

The app opens in your browser. It uses only the data inside the package, so it
works without an internet connection.

## Use the app

The sidebar has four controls. Each one changes the charts and tables.

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Sensor locations** | Choose up to three counting sensors, ideally the ones closest to your business or event. The sidebar lists where each sensor is. |
| **Years to compare** | Choose which years to draw on the typical-day chart. |
| **Type of day** | Switch between weekdays (Monday to Friday) and weekends. |
| **Same vertical scale** | Off, each sensor gets its own scale, which shows the shape of the day. On, scales match so you can see which sensor is busiest. |

The app has three tabs:

1. **When is it busiest?** shows the typical hour-by-hour pattern of foot
   traffic and a table with the busiest hour for each sensor and year.
2. **Change since 2025** shows each sensor's average daily foot traffic as a
   percentage of the baseline year.
3. **Fields and notes** explains every field and lists things to keep in mind.

If a choice leaves nothing to show, for example no sensor is chosen, the app
shows a message that says what to change.

## Interpret the outputs

### When is it busiest?

Each line is the average count in each hour of a typical day. The highest point
is when most people pass the sensor, which is a good guide to when to be open
and fully staffed. If a later year's line sits lower than the baseline year's
line, fewer people pass at that time. If the peak moves to a different hour,
the best time to reach customers has shifted.

### Change since the baseline year

Each point is a sensor's average daily foot traffic, as a percentage of the
baseline year. The dashed line at 100 is the baseline level. Points below it
mean fewer people than in the baseline year, and points above it mean more.

## Use the functions in R

The functions behind the app can be used directly. First, find the sensor with
the most recorded days:

```{r sensor}
library(melbfoot)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

top_sensor <- ped_hourly |>
  group_by(location_id, sensor_name) |>
  summarise(days = sum(n_days), .groups = "drop") |>
  slice_max(days, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

top_sensor
```

`hourly_profile()` returns the typical weekday for that sensor in every year:

```{r profile}
profile <- hourly_profile(
  sensors = top_sensor$location_id,
  years = unique(ped_hourly$year),
  day = "Weekday"
)

ggplot(profile, aes(hour, mean_count, colour = factor(year))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    x = "Hour of day (0 = midnight)",
    y = "Average pedestrians per hour",
    colour = "Year",
    title = top_sensor$sensor_name
  )
```

The busiest hour in each year:

```{r peak}
profile |>
  group_by(year) |>
  slice_max(mean_count, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  select(year, hour, mean_count, n_days)
```

`change_index()` compares each year's average daily traffic with a baseline
year. A value of 100 means the same as the baseline, and 110 means 10% more
people:

```{r change}
change_index(top_sensor$location_id)
```

## Things to keep in mind

- A count is a person passing a sensor, so the same person can be counted more
  than once. These are not unique visitors.
- The charts show averages for a typical day, not totals for a particular day.
- To make years comparable, the package keeps only 1 January to 2 November in
  each year. Only two years are available, so the change shows a one-year
  difference and not a long-term trend.
- Some sensors have gaps because they were added, moved or switched off.
  Averages built from fewer than 10 days are left out.
- Foot traffic is one input to a decision. It does not show how much people
  spend or why they were there.

## Data source

City of Melbourne, [Pedestrian Counting System (counts per
hour)](https://data.melbourne.vic.gov.au/explore/dataset/pedestrian-counting-system-monthly-counts-per-hour/)
and [Sensor
Locations](https://data.melbourne.vic.gov.au/explore/dataset/pedestrian-counting-system-sensor-locations/),
from the City of Melbourne Open Data Portal. The code that builds the packaged
data is in `data-raw/ped_data.R`.
